To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the mind and brain are embodied, embedded, enactive and extended.

1) the human being is an embodied and situated cognitive agent, 2) the human being lives in an intersubjective world, 3) the human being has an Ecology of Mind, 4) the human being can think, feel and act.
the mind is embodied, embedded, extended, enactive, affective and social.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: How can we study the mind as an embodied, embedded, extended and situated phenomenon?
the study of the human mind in its natural environment, and with the development of experimental methods to study the human mind in the context of culture and social interaction.
the following questions: How can we better understand the mind?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we are in the middle of a paradigm shift in the cognitive sciences.
we need to move beyond Computational Cognitivist models of mind, in order to better understand the nature of human cognition.
we are still far from understanding the nature and origin of intentionality, but that the research programs presented here constitute a step forward in this direction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the essays included in this special issue present an attempt to go beyond the computationalist approach of the mind and to move towards a more comprehensive and integrative view of human cognition.
, in the study of the mind, the time has come to move beyond computational cognitivism.
we are trying to understand the human brain and mind as a whole, as a complex system, and not as the sum of its parts.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to develop new methodological approaches to understand human cognition in all its complexity.

the study of intention and intersubjectivity, in their complexity and specificity, requires the integration of a number of different disciplines and methodological approaches, in order to overcome the limitations of the classical computationalist view of the mind.

we need to move beyond computational cognitivism and its radical individualism, towards a more holistic and embodied approach to mind, where the human being can be understood in the context of the social and natural world.
